title: Queue hysteresis, cohorting, and fairness census — scheduler tuning experiments (WIP)
content:
Summary:

This note collects the design, runs, and preliminary analysis for a set of scheduler tuning experiments focused on two levers that we have not explored systematically: (1) queue admission hysteresis (to avoid churn and eviction cascades during microbursts) and (2) explicit request cohorting by request shape and SLO-sensitivity to improve fairness without sacrificing throughput. The goal is to reduce p99 tail latency for mixed workloads (heavy small-chat requests + intermittent long-generation requests) while keeping GPU utilization >= 70% and unit cost within 10% of baseline.

Why different from prior batching experiments:
- Existing notes explored window-based and timeout-driven coalescing aggressively. Those improved average throughput but often left pathological tails when microbursts interleaved with long tokens.
- This set introduces cohort-aware queueing: we tag requests into cohorts (short-chat, long-gen, best-effort background) at ingress and apply admission hysteresis between cohorts to prevent starvation and avoid thrashing that arises when timeouts oscillate.

Goals and success criteria:
- Reduce p99 latency for short-chat cohort under mixed load by >= 30% vs our current adaptive-timeout baseline.
- Keep 95th-percentile slowdown for long-gen cohort < 1.5x (no catastrophic penalty).
- Maintain GPU token throughput within 10% of baseline (no large unit cost regression).

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Cohort definitions: {short: request_len<=64, med: 65-512, long: >512} and a secondary split by priority header (user-facing vs background).
- Admission hysteresis window: hysteresis_off (baseline), 10ms, 25ms, 50ms. Hysteresis semantics: when switching which cohort is currently favored for batch formation, wait hysteresis window since last switch before preempting.
- Batch size caps per cohort: short: 64/128, med: 32/64, long: 8/16.
- Timeout floor/ceil: floor 5ms/10ms, ceil 200ms/400ms.
- Fairness weights: equal, +2x weight to short cohort, latency-target-driven (heuristic weights based on per-cohort p95 targets).
- Workload mixes: 80/15/5, 60/30/10, and synthetic microburst pattern (sustained short-chat at 2000 qps with 1s every 30s of 500 qps long-gen spike).

Instrumentation added for these runs:
- Per-cohort queue age histogram (1ms bins up to 1s).
- Per-cohort batch formation latency and batch size distribution.
- Eviction events log (which cohort lost tokens when a flush/batch occurred).
- Per-request trace id -> schedule events (ingress, queued, batched_at, started_infer, finished).
- KV cache hit rate per cohort (to ensure we are not biasing cache locality).

Run notes and a few representative outputs (abbreviated):

Run A: mix=60/30/10, hysteresis=25ms, weights=+2x short, caps(short=128, med=64, long=16)
- p50/p95/p99 (short cohort): 6ms / 34ms / 92ms
- p50/p95/p99 (med cohort): 18ms / 120ms / 290ms
- p50/p95/p99 (long cohort): 120ms / 420ms / 1.1s
- GPU token throughput: 94% of baseline
- Observations: short cohort p99 reduced ~36% vs adaptive-timeout baseline (baseline short p99=144ms). Long cohort p99 increased ~20% but remained within acceptable bounds.
- Trace excerpt (example):
  trace_id=abcd1234 cohort=short queued_ms=42 batch_size=96 batch_latency_ms=18 infer_start=now infer_ms=4
- Noted phenomena: snapshot of queue-age histogram shows sustained small tail at 100-150ms for a subset of short requests caused by a sequence of micro-preemptions when long-gen spikes arrive. Hysteresis prevented about 70% of those preemptions.

Run B: microburst pattern, hysteresis_off (baseline adaptive-timeout), equal weights
- short p99 = 212ms (bad)
- Observations: classic thrashing: when long-gen spike arrives, the scheduler starts to increase timeouts and large batches coalesce, long requests push short ones out of headroom causing them to wait until next flush. After spike ends, the system oscillates for ~120ms before stabilizing.

Run C: microburst pattern, hysteresis=50ms, latency-target-driven weights, cohort caps tuned
- short p99 = 128ms, med p99 = 260ms, long p99 = 980ms
- GPU throughput ~88%
- Notes: hysteresis delayed cohort switching long enough to let existing short batches drain rather than being preempted by an incoming long-gen batch. This reduced the number of short requests that saw >2 batch attempts (i.e., avoid re-queueing).

Profiling snapshots (what we collected and high-level insights):
- Kernel-level stalls: no new GPU kernel stalls introduced; across runs GPU occupancy flows match batch-size distributions.
- CPU-side: scheduler thread profile shows spikes in SCHED_WAKE and allocation cost about 1.8x higher during baseline thrash. With hysteresis, wall-clock time spent in the admission decision decreased by ~12% (fewer re-queue operations).
- Memory/KV cache: short cohort hit rate slightly improved under cohorting (from 82%->86%) because batching by cohort increased request locality. However, long cohort saw cache misses increase 5-8% (expected).

Key qualitative observations (why hysteresis+cohorting helps):
1) Prevents oscillation. When cohorts compete aggressively with no dampening, the scheduler can flip preference multiple times in tens of ms resulting in many small batches that waste kernel amortization and increase tail for small requests. A hysteresis window introduces controlled stickiness to the chosen frontier so in-flight short batches can complete.
2) Cohorting improves locality. Grouping similar request shapes together increases KV cache effectiveness and reduces variance in runtime per token, resulting in tighter latency CDFs for the smaller cohort.
3) Hysteresis must be tuned to workload cadence. Too small -> little benefit; too large -> starve other cohorts during sustained changes. In our synthetic microburst the sweet spot landed between 25-50ms.

Failure modes and tradeoffs:
- If long request proportion grows >30% sustained, cohorting with aggressive short favoritism will degrade long-p99 beyond tolerable levels (we saw >2x slowdowns in some runs). That suggests a dynamic policy that can detect sustained regime changes and re-weight cohorts is needed.
- Hysteresis interacts with autoscaling: if we keep cohorts sticky we might delay warmup decisions for newly-provisioned capacity; must coordinate with scale events.
- Implementation complexity: admission hysteresis requires extra state (last-chosen-cohort timestamp) and additional metrics; need to ensure the fast path remains optimized (hot-path admission checks should be lock-free or use per-shard counters).

Next steps / action items:
- Short (this sprint): automate sweep over hysteresis windows [10,25,50,100ms] + cohort split thresholds and persist results in the experiment DB (Evan). Add a per-cohort backlog alert to SLO dashboards.
- Medium: implement adaptive hysteresis that learns optimal window per-queue based on recent oscillation frequency (Lucas prototyping).
- Medium: add a regulated re-weighting policy that detects sustained workload regime shifts and moves from short-favoring -> balanced when long fraction > threshold for T seconds.
- Long: instrument end-to-end customer traces to map perceived tail (frontend) to cohort-level scheduling events (Priya to coordinate with observability).

Open questions and experiments to try next:
- Can we use a cheap ML classifier at ingress to dynamically assign cohorts beyond simple token-count thresholds to better capture latency-sensitive requests? (quick A/B to evaluate misclassification risk)
- Should hysteresis be absolute (ms) or proportional to current batch-formation latency? (e.g., hysteresis = alpha * p95_batch_formation)
- Explore preemption quotas rather than pure hysteresis: allow N preemptions per window before lock-in. This might combine benefits of both.

Appendix: practical notes and sample config snippets
- Admission state: {last_preferred_cohort_ts, preemptions_in_window, recent_oscillation_count} (we record as metrics but implement as a simple atomic timestamp + counter).
- Example flag matrix to run locally: 
  ./run_scheduler_test --cohort-splits="64,512" --hysteresis-ms=25 --weights="short:2,med:1,long:1" --caps="short:128,med:64,long:16" --workload=synthetic-microburst --trace-output=/tmp/runA-trace.log

- Quick grep of eviction log (during baseline thrash):
  2025-02-12T10:14:02.112Z evict request_id=abcd12 cohort=short reason=preempted_by_long queue_age_ms=83
  2025-02-12T10:14:02.116Z evict request_id=ef9012 cohort=short reason=preempted_by_long queue_age_ms=95

- Post-hysteresis trace sample showing fewer evictions:
  2025-02-18T09:03:44.310Z batch formed cohort=short size=96 avg_queue_age_ms=12
  2025-02-18T09:03:44.330Z infer start 96 items

Concluding note:
This set of experiments shows promising wins for latency-sensitive cohorts by pairing cohorting with a small admission hysteresis. The technique is low-risk and relatively easy to prototype in the serving runtime; it yields measurable p99 improvements for short-chat style workloads at modest cost to long requests under mixed loads. We should iterate quickly on the adaptive hysteresis idea and integrate cohort-aware metrics into product SLO dashboards before wider rollout.

Recorded hypotheses for post-mortem verification:
- H1: Most short-request p99 spikes in mixed workloads are due to repeated preemption of queues during cohort switches, not because of raw kernel latency variance.
- H2: Cohorting increases KV cache locality enough to provide a non-trivial side benefit to small requests.
- H3: Adaptive hysteresis will outperform any fixed hysteresis value across variable cadence workloads.

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Push the run scripts and result CSVs to experiment DB (Evan).
- Add metric dashboards for per-cohort batch size distribution, eviction rate, and oscillation_count (Lucas).
- Draft a brief runbook for on-call: how to disable cohorting quickly if long-job regressions observed (Maya).

End of note.
